title: Syllogism
summary: Syllogism questions hand you 2-3 statements (All / No / Some / Some-not / Only-a-few) as true and ask which conclusions follow. The reliable method is minimal-diagram plus counter-example hunting: draw the least-committal picture, then try to break each conclusion — a conclusion follows only if no valid diagram breaks it. Modern twists (possibility conclusions, either-or complementary pairs, 'only a few') all reduce to the same discipline with one twist: possibility needs just one supporting diagram, and either-or needs the two conclusions to be exact negations.

subtopics.title: What a syllogism is and how to test it
subtopics.concept:
A syllogism gives two or three statements that you must accept as true. Then you judge conclusions. A conclusion follows only if it holds in **every** picture that fits the statements.

Real-world facts do not matter. Try to break each conclusion with one picture.

formulas.name: Transitivity of All
formulas.tex: A \subset B \wedge B \subset C \Rightarrow A \subset C
formulas.note: 'All A are B + All B are C → All A are C' is the only freely chained rule.

formulas.name: Conversion of All
formulas.note: Valid (classes are assumed non-empty): 'Some B are A' follows.

formulas.name: Conversion of No / Some
formulas.tex: \text{No } A \cap B \Leftrightarrow \text{No } B \cap A;\quad \text{Some } A \cap B \Leftrightarrow \text{Some } B \cap A

tricks.title: Find the shared term
tricks.body: The conclusion must join the two outer terms. Find the term that appears in both statements, and ask what travels through it.

example.q: All pens are books. Some books are files. Does 'Some pens are files' follow?
steps: The shared term is books.
The files that are books may not be pens.
Draw the file-books outside pens.

tricks.title: One counter-picture kills it
tricks.body: You do not need to prove a conclusion. You need only one picture that fits the statements and breaks it.

mistakes.wrong: Rejecting a statement because it is false in real life.
mistakes.right: Accept every statement as true. Reason only from the statements.

mistakes.wrong: Reading 'All A are B' as 'All B are A'.
mistakes.right: All does not reverse. Only 'Some B are A' follows.

mistakes.wrong: Joining two 'Some' statements into a conclusion.
mistakes.right: Two 'Some' statements never join. Draw the overlaps apart to test.

mistakes.wrong: Passing a 'Some-not' through an All.
mistakes.right: The A outside B may or may not be a C. Nothing follows.

mistakes.wrong: Drawing the picture that supports the conclusion.
mistakes.right: Draw the smallest picture that fits the statements. Then try to break the conclusion.

subtopics.notes:
### What a syllogism asks
You get two or three statements. Accept them as true, even when they sound silly. Then you get conclusions to judge.

A conclusion **follows** only if it is true in every picture that fits the statements. One picture that breaks it is enough to reject it.

> **Rule:** Assume every group named in the statements has at least one member.

### The four statement forms
| Statement | Meaning |
|---|---|
| All A are B | Every A is inside B. B may be bigger. |
| No A are B | A and B never meet. |
| Some A are B | At least one member is in both. |
| Some A are not B | At least one A lies outside B. |

**All** and **No** describe the whole group. **Some** only promises that one member exists. That makes conclusions built on 'some' easy to break.

### Safe reversals
| Statement | Reversal that follows |
|---|---|
| All A are B | Some B are A |
| No A are B | No B are A |
| Some A are B | Some B are A |
| Some A are not B | none |

> **Watch:** 'All A are B' does not give 'All B are A'. 'Some A are not B' does not give 'Some B are not A'.

### Chains that work
- All A are B and All B are C give **All A are C**.
- Some A are B and All B are C give **Some A are C**.
- All A are B and No B are C give **No A are C**.
- No A are B and Some B are C give **Some C are not A**.

### Chains that do not work
- Two 'Some' statements never join. Some A are B and Some B are C give nothing about A and C.
- A 'Some-not' does not pass through an All. The A that is outside B may or may not be a C.

### Try to break the conclusion
Do not draw a picture that helps the conclusion. Draw the smallest picture that fits the statements. Then ask whether you can move one group to make the conclusion false.

If you can, the conclusion fails. If you cannot, it follows.

### Reading the options
Judge conclusion I and conclusion II separately. Then look at the options.

- Only I follows: II can be broken.
- Only II follows: I can be broken.
- Both follow: neither can be broken.
- Neither follows: both can be broken.

Never let one conclusion influence the other. Each one has its own test.

### A worked example
**Statements**
- Some pens are books.
- All books are files.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some pens are files.
- II. All pens are files.

**Options**
- (A) Only I follows
- (B) Only II follows
- (C) Both I and II follow
- (D) Neither I nor II follows

**Solution**
- The shared term is books. The pen that is a book is also a file, so I follows.
- For II, draw one pen outside books. All statements still hold, so II fails.

Answer: **(A) Only I follows**.

patterns.name: Some + All chain (shared member travels)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Some A are B' then 'All B are C' (or the other order). One conclusion links A and C.
steps: Find the term that both statements share.
The guaranteed A-and-B member is a B, so it is also a C.
So 'Some A are C' follows.
Test the other conclusion by drawing a counter-picture.
patterns.why: The member we are sure of travels through the All.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Some pens are books.
- All books are files.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some pens are files.
- II. All pens are files.

**Options**
- (A) Only I follows
- (B) Only II follows
- (C) Both I and II follow
- (D) Neither I nor II follows
steps: The shared term is books. The pen that is a book is also a file, so I follows.
For II, draw one pen outside books. All statements still hold, so II fails.

patterns.name: All-chain with a conversion conclusion
patterns.howToSpot: Two 'All' statements form a chain. One conclusion turns the chain around.
steps: Chain the All statements: A inside B inside C.
'All A are C' follows.
'Some C are A' also follows.
Reject 'All C are A'. The chain never runs backwards.
patterns.why: Containment carries forward, and the reverse needs new information.

example.q:
**Statements**
- All rings are coins.
- All coins are metals.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some metals are rings.
- II. All metals are rings.

**Options**
- (A) Only II follows
- (B) Both I and II follow
- (C) Neither I nor II follows
- (D) Only I follows
steps: Chain the All statements: rings sit inside coins, and coins sit inside metals.
So all rings are metals, and the reverse form 'Some metals are rings' follows too.
II runs the chain backwards. A metal that is not a coin breaks it, so II fails.

patterns.name: No + Some gives Some-not
patterns.howToSpot: 'No A are B' and 'Some B are C'. The conclusion is about C and A.
steps: Find the shared class B.
The B-and-C member cannot be an A.
So 'Some C are not A' follows.
Reject stronger claims such as 'No C are A'.
patterns.why: The shared member inherits B's total exile from A.

example.q:
**Statements**
- No walls are doors.
- Some doors are gates.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some gates are not walls.
- II. No gates are walls.

**Options**
- (A) Both I and II follow
- (B) Neither I nor II follows
- (C) Only I follows
- (D) Only II follows
steps: The shared term is doors. A gate that is a door cannot be a wall, so I follows.
For II, a gate that is not a door might still be a wall. So II fails.

patterns.name: Conversion-only pair
patterns.howToSpot: One statement and two conclusions. One is its plain reversal, and the other overreaches it.
steps: Recall the safe reversals: All gives Some. Some and No reverse both ways.
The reversal follows.
The other conclusion adds a new claim. Reject it.
patterns.why: A reversal only swaps the terms. It never adds new information.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Some tables are chairs.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some chairs are tables.
- II. All chairs are tables.

**Options**
- (A) Neither I nor II follows
- (B) Only I follows
- (C) Only II follows
- (D) Both I and II follow
steps: 'Some' converts freely, so I follows.
II adds a new claim about every chair. The statement never says that.

patterns.name: Three-statement chain
patterns.howToSpot: Three statements link four groups in a line, mostly All and No.
steps: Chain the All statements from the left.
Carry the chain through the group named in the No statement.
Anything inside that group is also cut off from the last group.
Remember to reverse a No statement freely.
patterns.why: Everything inside a group inherits that group's No relation.

example.q:
**Statements**
- All cups are plates.
- All plates are bowls.
- No bowls are jars.

**Conclusions**
- I. No cups are jars.
- II. No jars are plates.

**Options**
- (A) Only I follows
- (B) Only II follows
- (C) Both I and II follow
- (D) Neither I nor II follows
steps: Chain the first two: cups sit inside plates, and plates sit inside bowls.
No bowl is a jar, so nothing inside bowls can be a jar. Cups and plates are inside bowls.
That gives both I and II, because 'No' reads the same in both directions.

patterns.name: Some-not does not travel
patterns.howToSpot: 'Some A are not B' with 'All B are C'. The conclusions are about A and C.
steps: Find the outside member: an A that is not a B.
Ask whether it must be a C. Nothing forces it in or out.
Draw it outside C, then draw it inside C.
Neither conclusion is forced.
patterns.why: The All statement covers B only. It says nothing about members outside B.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Some birds are not pets.
- All pets are animals.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some birds are not animals.
- II. No birds are animals.

**Options**
- (A) Only II follows
- (B) Both I and II follow
- (C) Neither I nor II follows
- (D) Only I follows
steps: The bird outside pets is the only bird we are sure of.
That bird may or may not be an animal. Nothing links it to animals.
So I and II both fail. A 'Some-not' does not travel through an All.

patterns.name: Two Some statements
patterns.howToSpot: 'Some A are B' and 'Some B are C'. Conclusions link A and C.
steps: Note that the two overlaps may involve different members of B.
Draw them apart.
Test both conclusions in that picture.
Neither follows.
patterns.why: A 'Some' promises one member. Two promises can point to different members.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Some boxes are bags.
- Some bags are sacks.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some boxes are sacks.
- II. Some sacks are boxes.

**Options**
- (A) Both I and II follow
- (B) Neither I nor II follows
- (C) Only I follows
- (D) Only II follows
steps: The box that is a bag and the bag that is a sack can be different bags.
Draw the two overlaps apart. Boxes and sacks never meet.
Two 'Some' statements never join. Neither conclusion follows.

revision: Accept the statements as true. A conclusion follows only if it holds in every picture.
All converts to Some. No and Some convert both ways. Some-not does not convert.
Chains that work: All+All, Some+All, All+No, No+Some (gives Some-not).
Two 'Some' statements never join. A 'Some-not' does not pass through an All.
Draw the smallest picture and try to break the conclusion with one counter-picture.
Assume every named group has at least one member.

subtopics.title: Possibility conclusions
subtopics.concept:
A possibility conclusion asks a lighter question: can this be true without breaking a statement? One supporting picture is enough to make it follow.

It fails only when a statement makes it impossible.

tricks.title: Defence lawyer thinking
tricks.body: For a possibility, flip your mindset. Build one picture where it holds. Done.

mistakes.wrong: Looking for a picture where the possibility must hold.
mistakes.right: You need only one picture where it can hold.

mistakes.wrong: Ignoring the 'No' statement when you draw the possibility.
mistakes.right: A 'No' statement blocks every picture that puts a member across it.

mistakes.wrong: Saying 'No B are A' is possible after 'All A are B'.
mistakes.right: Groups are non-empty. A member of A is a member of B, so B and A must meet.

mistakes.wrong: Saying 'All A are B' is possible after 'Only a few A are B'.
mistakes.right: Only a few guarantees an A outside B, so that possibility is dead.

mistakes.wrong: Judging a definite conclusion by the one-picture rule.
mistakes.right: A definite conclusion must hold in every picture.

subtopics.notes:
### What a possibility conclusion asks
A definite conclusion says: this **must** be true. A possibility conclusion says: this **can** be true.

You are now looking for one picture only. If some picture fits every statement and also makes the possibility true, the possibility follows.

> **Rule:** For a possibility, one supporting picture is enough. It follows unless a statement blocks it.

### The one-picture method
1. Read the possibility as a request. For example: can I put all buses inside cars?
2. Try to draw it. Keep every statement true, especially every overlap.
3. If you can, it follows. If every attempt collides with a statement, it fails.

### What blocks a possibility
- **A No statement.** If no desk is a shelf, then no table inside desks can be a shelf.
- **A forced overlap.** If every lion is a cat, no cat can fail to be a lion in all cases. 'No cat is a lion' is impossible.
- **Only a few.** 'Only a few A are B' rules out 'All A are B'. It also rules out 'No A are B'.

> **Watch:** Groups are never empty. So a possibility that empties a group always fails.

### What stays possible
Most other cases stay possible. From 'Some A are B', all of these can be true: all A are B, all B are A, some A are not B.

From 'Only a few A are B', 'All B are A' is still possible. Draw B inside A and keep one A outside.

### Two conclusions together
Often one conclusion is a possibility and the other is definite. Judge them by different standards. The definite one needs every picture. The possibility needs one picture.

Then match the pair to the options: only I, only II, both or neither.

### Words that signal a possibility
Look for 'is a possibility', 'may be true' or 'can be true'. These words change the question from 'must' to 'can'.

Without them, treat the conclusion as definite.

### A quick self-check
After you pick an answer, test it once. If you said a possibility fails, name the statement that blocks it. If you said it follows, name the picture that shows it.

Both answers should be easy to say in one sentence.

### A worked example
**Statements**
- Some cars are trucks.
- Some trucks are buses.

**Conclusions**
- I. All buses being cars is a possibility.
- II. No cars are buses.

**Options**
- (A) Only I follows
- (B) Only II follows
- (C) Both I and II follow
- (D) Neither I nor II follows

**Solution**
- For I, draw all buses inside cars. The car-truck overlap and the truck-bus overlap still hold. So I follows.
- For II, cars and buses may overlap. So 'No car is a bus' is not forced, and II fails.

Answer: **(A) Only I follows**.

patterns.name: Plain possibility (nothing blocks it)
patterns.howToSpot: The words 'is a possibility' appear, and no 'No' statement touches the two terms.
steps: Try to draw the possibility around the statements.
Keep every 'Some' overlap alive.
If one clean picture survives, the possibility follows.
patterns.why: A possibility needs one consistent picture, not every picture.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Some cars are trucks.
- Some trucks are buses.

**Conclusions**
- I. All buses being cars is a possibility.
- II. No cars are buses.

**Options**
- (A) Only I follows
- (B) Only II follows
- (C) Both I and II follow
- (D) Neither I nor II follows
steps: For I, draw all buses inside cars. The car-truck overlap and the truck-bus overlap still hold. So I follows.
For II, cars and buses may overlap. So 'No car is a bus' is not forced, and II fails.

patterns.name: Possibility blocked by a No statement
patterns.howToSpot: A 'No X are Y' statement, and a possibility that would push X members into Y.
steps: Trace the members that are sure to exist.
Ask if the possibility would force one of them across the 'No'.
If yes, the possibility fails.
Test the partner conclusion separately.
patterns.why: A 'No' statement allows no crossing, whatever the picture.

example.q:
**Statements**
- All tables are desks.
- No desks are shelves.

**Conclusions**
- I. All shelves being tables is a possibility.
- II. No shelves are tables.

**Options**
- (A) Only II follows
- (B) Both I and II follow
- (C) Neither I nor II follows
- (D) Only I follows
steps: Tables sit inside desks, and no desk is a shelf. So no table can be a shelf. II follows.
For I, all shelves would sit inside tables, and so inside desks. That breaks 'No desk is a shelf'. I fails.

patterns.name: Possibility with only-a-few statements
patterns.howToSpot: 'Only a few A are B' and a possibility about A, B or a third group.
steps: Split it into Some and Some-not.
'All A are B' is now impossible.
Try to draw the other possibilities, such as 'All B are A'.
Keep the ones you can draw.
patterns.why: Only-a-few fixes the A side and leaves the B side open.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Only a few lamps are bulbs.

**Conclusions**
- I. All lamps being bulbs is a possibility.
- II. All bulbs being lamps is a possibility.

**Options**
- (A) Only II follows
- (B) Both I and II follow
- (C) Neither I nor II follows
- (D) Only I follows
steps: 'Only a few lamps are bulbs' means some lamps are bulbs and some lamps are not bulbs.
I asks for all lamps to be bulbs. The lamp that is not a bulb blocks it.
II asks for all bulbs to be lamps. Draw bulbs inside lamps and keep one lamp outside. It works, so II follows.

patterns.name: Possibility paired with a definite conclusion
patterns.howToSpot: One conclusion is a possibility. The other is a definite claim.
steps: Test the definite one with a counter-picture.
Build one picture for the possibility.
Match the two results to the options.
patterns.why: The two halves use different standards.

example.q:
**Statements**
- All ships are boats.
- Some boats are rafts.

**Conclusions**
- I. All rafts being ships is a possibility.
- II. Some ships are rafts.

**Options**
- (A) Both I and II follow
- (B) Neither I nor II follows
- (C) Only I follows
- (D) Only II follows
steps: For I, draw rafts inside ships, and ships inside boats. The boat-raft overlap still exists. So I follows.
II is a definite claim. The raft that is a boat may not be a ship. So II fails.

patterns.name: Possibility that empties a group
patterns.howToSpot: After 'All A are B', a possibility such as 'No B are A'.
steps: Remember that every group has at least one member.
Every A is a B, so B and A meet.
Any possibility that separates them fails.
patterns.why: If groups cannot be empty, an All statement forces an overlap.

example.q:
**Statements**
- All lions are cats.

**Conclusions**
- I. No cats being lions is a possibility.
- II. Some cats being lions is a possibility.

**Options**
- (A) Neither I nor II follows
- (B) Only I follows
- (C) Only II follows
- (D) Both I and II follow
steps: Every lion is a cat, and lions exist. So at least one cat is a lion.
I needs no cat to be a lion. That is impossible, so I fails.
II is already true in every picture. So it is certainly possible.

revision: A possibility needs one supporting picture. A definite conclusion needs every picture.
A 'No' statement blocks a possibility that pushes a member across it.
Groups are non-empty. 'All A are B' makes 'No B are A' impossible.
'Only a few A are B' rules out 'All A are B' but leaves 'All B are A' possible.
Judge a mixed pair by different standards. Then match the options.

subtopics.title: Either-or (complementary pairs)
subtopics.concept:
Sometimes neither conclusion follows on its own, but they are exact opposites. Then one of them is true in every picture, and the answer is 'Either I or II follows'.

Only two shapes of pairs qualify. Always test each conclusion alone first.

tricks.title: Spot the opposite pair
tricks.body: Look for (All, Some-not) or (Some, No) on the same two terms. Then test each alone.

example.q: I. Some shirts are red. II. No shirts are red. The statements never mention red. Answer?
steps: Same terms, and the pair is Some and No.
Neither follows alone.
So one of them holds in every picture.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing either-or when one conclusion follows alone.
mistakes.right: Test each conclusion alone first. If one follows, choose 'Only I' or 'Only II'.

mistakes.wrong: Treating 'No' and 'Some-not' as an opposite pair.
mistakes.right: They can both be false. Only (All, Some-not) and (Some, No) are opposites.

mistakes.wrong: Pairing conclusions that use different terms.
mistakes.right: Both conclusions must use the same two terms.

mistakes.wrong: Treating 'All' and 'No' as a pair.
mistakes.right: Both are false when A only partly overlaps B.

mistakes.wrong: Skipping the pair check because the statements are long.
mistakes.right: Extra statements only matter in the alone test. The pair shape decides the rest.

subtopics.notes:
### What an either-or pair is
Sometimes neither conclusion follows on its own, but the two conclusions are exact opposites. Then one of them is true in every picture. The answer is **Either I or II follows**.

This is logic, not luck. If two conclusions are negations of each other, no picture can make both false.

### The two legal pairs
Both conclusions must use the **same two terms**, in either order.

| Pair | Why it covers every case |
|---|---|
| All A are B and Some A are not B | Either every A is inside B, or one A is outside. |
| Some A are B and No A are B | Either A and B meet, or they do not. |

### The three-step test
1. Check the pair. Same two terms? One of the two legal shapes? If not, there is no either-or.
2. Test each conclusion alone. If one follows, the answer is 'Only I' or 'Only II'.
3. If neither follows alone, the answer is 'Either I or II follows'.

> **Rule:** Always do step 2 before step 3. A conclusion that follows alone rules out either-or.

### Pairs that look right but are not
- **Different terms.** 'All A are B' and 'Some A are not C' are not opposites.
- **No and Some-not.** Both can be false. A group inside B has some A in B, but no A outside B.
- **All and No.** Both can be false when A partly overlaps B.
- **Some and Some-not.** Both can be true together, so exams do not treat them as a pair.

> **Watch:** Two conclusions that are both false at the same time are never an either-or pair.

### Extra statements
With three statements, ignore the extra one while you check the pair shape. It matters only in step 2, where it may prove one conclusion alone.

### Where it shows up in the options
The option 'Either I or II follows' appears only when the answer is truly either-or. If you see it, do not pick it by habit.

Check the pair shape and run the alone test before you choose it.

### Why the pairs work
Take 'All A are B' and 'Some A are not B'. A is either entirely inside B or not. There is no third case.

Take 'Some A are B' and 'No A are B'. The two groups either share a member or they share none. Again there is no third case.

### A worked example
**Statements**
- All keys are metals.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some keys are iron.
- II. No keys are iron.

**Options**
- (A) Either I or II follows
- (B) Neither I nor II follows
- (C) Only I follows
- (D) Only II follows

**Solution**
- Same two terms: keys and iron. The pair is 'Some' and 'No'.
- The statement does not link keys to iron, so neither follows alone.
- Keys and iron either share a member or do not. One of the two is always true.

Answer: **(A) Either I or II follows**.

patterns.name: (All, Some-not) complementary pair
patterns.howToSpot: Conclusions 'All A are B' and 'Some A are not B'. The same two terms, and neither follows alone.
steps: Check that the terms match.
Test each conclusion alone.
If neither follows, choose 'Either I or II'.
patterns.why: A is either wholly inside B or partly outside. No third case exists.

example.q:
**Statements**
- All rings are metals.
- Some metals are heavy.

**Conclusions**
- I. All rings are heavy.
- II. Some rings are not heavy.

**Options**
- (A) Only I follows
- (B) Only II follows
- (C) Either I or II follows
- (D) Neither I nor II follows
steps: Same two terms: rings and heavy. The pair is 'All' and 'Some-not'.
Test each alone. The statements do not fix how rings relate to heavy. Neither follows alone.
Either every ring is heavy, or some ring is not. Nothing else can happen.

patterns.name: (Some, No) complementary pair
patterns.howToSpot: Conclusions 'Some A are B' and 'No A are B' on the same two terms.
steps: Check the terms and the pair shape.
Test each alone.
If neither follows, choose either-or.
patterns.why: Two groups either share a member or they do not.

example.q:
**Statements**
- All keys are metals.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some keys are iron.
- II. No keys are iron.

**Options**
- (A) Either I or II follows
- (B) Neither I nor II follows
- (C) Only I follows
- (D) Only II follows
steps: Same two terms: keys and iron. The pair is 'Some' and 'No'.
The statement does not link keys to iron, so neither follows alone.
Keys and iron either share a member or do not. One of the two is always true.

patterns.name: Fake complementary pair
patterns.howToSpot: The conclusions look like a pair but use different terms, or use (No, Some-not), or one follows alone.
steps: Compare the terms word by word.
Reject the (No, Some-not) shape.
If one conclusion follows alone, answer that one.
patterns.why: Both conclusions can be false together, so the either-or argument breaks.

example.q:
**Statements**
- All cups are dishes.
- Some dishes are pots.

**Conclusions**
- I. No cups are pots.
- II. Some cups are not pots.

**Options**
- (A) Neither I nor II follows
- (B) Only I follows
- (C) Only II follows
- (D) Both I and II follow
steps: The pair is 'No' and 'Some-not'. That is not a complementary pair.
Draw every cup inside pots. Then I fails, and II fails as well.
Both can be false together, so there is no either-or. The answer is neither.

patterns.name: Either-or with three statements
patterns.howToSpot: Three statements, but the two conclusions only ask about one pair of terms.
steps: Ignore the extra statements while you check the pair shape.
Test each conclusion alone. An extra statement might prove one.
If neither is proved, choose either-or.
patterns.why: The pair argument needs only the two conclusions.

example.q:
**Statements**
- All pens are books.
- No books are files.
- Some files are bags.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some bags are pens.
- II. No bags are pens.

**Options**
- (A) Only II follows
- (B) Either I or II follows
- (C) Neither I nor II follows
- (D) Only I follows
steps: The conclusions use bags and pens. They form the pair 'Some' and 'No'.
A bag can be a pen, and a bag can fail to be one. Neither follows alone.
The other statements do not settle the bags-pens link. So the answer is either-or.

patterns.name: One of the pair is provable
patterns.howToSpot: The conclusions form a legal pair, but the statements give a chain that settles one of them.
steps: Notice the legal pair.
Do not stop there. Test each conclusion alone first.
If one follows, answer 'Only' that one.
patterns.why: A conclusion that follows in every picture makes its opposite false in every picture.

example.q:
**Statements**
- All pens are books.
- All books are files.

**Conclusions**
- I. All pens are files.
- II. Some pens are not files.

**Options**
- (A) Only I follows
- (B) Only II follows
- (C) Both I and II follow
- (D) Neither I nor II follows
steps: The pair is 'All' and 'Some-not', so it looks like an either-or.
Test each alone first. Chain the statements: all pens are files. I follows.
Because I follows alone, the answer is 'Only I'. Never choose either-or here.

revision: Either-or needs neither conclusion alone and an exact opposite pair.
Legal pairs: (All, Some-not) and (Some, No), on the same two terms.
(No, Some-not) and (All, No) can both be false. They are not pairs.
Test each conclusion alone first. One that follows ends the either-or idea.
Extra statements do not change the pair shape.

subtopics.title: Only-a-few and definite-case rulings
subtopics.concept:
'Only a few A are B' means two things at once: some A are B and some A are not B. 'A few' and 'Many' mean plain 'Some'.

Split the statement first. Then treat it like any other syllogism.

tricks.title: Split on sight
tricks.body: Rewrite every 'Only a few A are B' as two lines: Some A are B, and Some A are not B. Then solve as normal.

mistakes.wrong: Reading 'A few' or 'Many' as 'only a few'.
mistakes.right: They mean plain 'Some'. No outside part is guaranteed.

mistakes.wrong: Assuming 'only a few A are B' says something about B outside A.
mistakes.right: It only fixes the A side. B outside A is undecided.

mistakes.wrong: Passing the outside-A member through 'All B are C'.
mistakes.right: Only the A-and-B member travels. The outside member may or may not be a C.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking 'only a few' allows 'All A are B'.
mistakes.right: It guarantees an A outside B, so 'All A are B' is false.

mistakes.wrong: Joining two only-a-few statements.
mistakes.right: The overlaps can be different members. Nothing joins.

subtopics.notes:
### What only a few really says
Modern papers use three phrases.

- **Some A are B**: at least one A is a B. Nothing more.
- **A few** and **Many A are B**: exactly the same as Some.
- **Only a few A are B**: two facts at once. Some A are B, and some A are not B.

So 'Only a few cups are plates' guarantees a cup outside plates. It says nothing about plates that are not cups.

> **Rule:** Split 'only a few' into two arrows. Feed both into your picture.

### What follows at once
From **Only a few A are B**:
- Some A are B follows.
- Some A are not B follows.
- All A are B is false.
- No A are B is false.
- Anything about B outside A is undecided.

### Combining with All
Take 'Only a few A are B' and 'All B are C'.
- Some A are C follows. The A that is a B is also a C.
- Some A are not C does **not** follow. The A outside B may still be a C.

> **Watch:** Only the A-and-B member travels through the All. The A-outside-B member does not.

### Combining with No
Take 'Only a few A are B' and 'No B are C'. Then some A are not C follows, because the A that is a B cannot be a C.

But 'All A are C' is impossible in this case. It would put that A into C.

### Two only-a-few statements
'Only a few A are B' and 'Only a few B are C' do not join. The A-and-B members and the B-and-C members can be different members.

### Three phrases side by side
| Phrase | Some A are B | Some A are not B |
|---|---|---|
| Some A are B | Yes | Not fixed |
| A few / Many A are B | Yes | Not fixed |
| Only a few A are B | Yes | Yes |

Only the last phrase guarantees the outside part. That is the whole difference between them. Do not read 'A few' or 'Many' as 'only a few'. They promise the overlap and nothing else.

### Checking with a picture
Draw the outside A member as a dot beside the B circle. Then ask whether the dot has to sit inside C. If it can sit either way, the conclusion is not forced.

Watch which side each conclusion is about. 'Some A are not B' talks about the A side. 'Some B are not A' talks about the B side.

'Only a few A are B' fixes the first and leaves the second open.

### A worked example
**Statements**
- Only a few cups are plates.
- All plates are bowls.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some cups are bowls.
- II. Some cups are not bowls.

**Options**
- (A) Neither I nor II follows
- (B) Only I follows
- (C) Only II follows
- (D) Both I and II follow

**Solution**
- The cup that is a plate is also a bowl. So I follows.
- The cup that is not a plate may still be a bowl. So II fails.

Answer: **(B) Only I follows**.

patterns.name: Only-a-few direct consequences
patterns.howToSpot: 'Only a few A are B', and conclusions quoting Some, Some-not, All or No on A and B.
steps: Rewrite as Some A are B and Some A are not B.
All A are B and No A are B are false.
Anything about B outside A is undecided.
patterns.why: Only-a-few welds two facts about the A side and says nothing about B.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Only a few pens are pencils.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some pens are not pencils.
- II. Some pencils are not pens.

**Options**
- (A) Only II follows
- (B) Both I and II follow
- (C) Neither I nor II follows
- (D) Only I follows
steps: Split the statement: some pens are pencils, and some pens are not pencils.
I is the second half, so it follows.
II is about pencils outside pens. The statement says nothing about that side. II fails.

patterns.name: Only-a-few + All chain
patterns.howToSpot: 'Only a few A are B' and 'All B are C'. Conclusions are about A and C.
steps: The A-and-B member is also a C, so 'Some A are C' follows.
The A outside B is not tied to C.
So 'Some A are not C' does not follow.
patterns.why: Only the B member travels through the All.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Only a few cups are plates.
- All plates are bowls.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some cups are bowls.
- II. Some cups are not bowls.

**Options**
- (A) Neither I nor II follows
- (B) Only I follows
- (C) Only II follows
- (D) Both I and II follow
steps: The cup that is a plate is also a bowl. So I follows.
The cup that is not a plate may still be a bowl. So II fails.

patterns.name: 'A few / Many' = plain Some
patterns.howToSpot: The statement says 'A few A are B' or 'Many A are B'. Students over-read it as only-a-few.
steps: Treat it exactly as 'Some A are B'.
No outside part is guaranteed.
Chain the Some member through any All.
patterns.why: 'A few' and 'Many' only promise that the overlap exists.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Some doctors are singers.
- All singers are dancers.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some doctors are dancers.
- II. Some doctors are not singers.

**Options**
- (A) Only I follows
- (B) Only II follows
- (C) Both I and II follow
- (D) Neither I nor II follows
steps: Treat 'A few' like 'Some'. Some doctors are singers, and every singer is a dancer.
So some doctors are dancers. I follows.
II needs a doctor outside singers. 'A few' does not guarantee it, so II fails.

patterns.name: Only-a-few with possibility and No statements
patterns.howToSpot: An only-a-few statement, a No statement and a mix of definite and possibility conclusions.
steps: Split only-a-few into Some and Some-not.
Trace the guaranteed member through the No statement.
Test each conclusion by its own standard.
patterns.why: The No statement can cut off the guaranteed member from a third group.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Only a few birds are pets.
- No pets are stones.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some birds are not stones.
- II. All birds being stones is a possibility.

**Options**
- (A) Both I and II follow
- (B) Neither I nor II follows
- (C) Only I follows
- (D) Only II follows
steps: Some birds are pets. A pet is never a stone. So some birds are not stones. I follows.
II asks for all birds to be stones. The bird that is a pet would have to be a stone. II fails.

patterns.name: Two only-a-few statements
patterns.howToSpot: 'Only a few A are B' and 'Only a few B are C', with conclusions about A and C.
steps: Split both statements.
The A-and-B members and B-and-C members may differ.
Draw the two overlaps apart.
Neither Some nor Some-not is forced.
patterns.why: Each only-a-few links one pair. Two links do not join.

example.q:
**Statements**
- Only a few trees are plants.
- Only a few plants are shrubs.

**Conclusions**
- I. Some trees are shrubs.
- II. Some trees are not shrubs.

**Options**
- (A) Only II follows
- (B) Both I and II follow
- (C) Neither I nor II follows
- (D) Only I follows
steps: Each 'only a few' gives some and some-not. The two links do not join up.
The trees that are plants may all be shrubs, or none of them may be. Neither claim is forced.

revision: Only a few A are B = Some A are B + Some A are not B.
A few and Many = plain Some. Nothing is guaranteed outside.
Only the A-and-B member travels through All B are C.
Only a few A are B makes 'All A are B' and 'No A are B' false.
Nothing is fixed about B outside A.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two statements like "All A are B" and "Some B are C", then conclusions.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Draw the smallest picture that fits the statements.
A conclusion follows only if it is true in every possible picture.

example.q: Statements: Some dogs are cats. All cats are rats. I. Some dogs are rats. II. All rats are dogs.
example.solution:
The dogs that are cats are also rats, so I follows
Rats can be outside the dogs, so II does not follow
Answer: **only I**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Three statements (All, Some or No) and conclusions that need the whole chain.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Join the "All" links first.
Follow the "Some" part through each statement.

example.q: Statements: All keys are locks. Some locks are doors. No door is a window. I. Some keys are doors. II. Some locks are not windows.
example.solution:
The locks that are doors may not be keys, so I does not follow
Those locks are doors, and no door is a window, so II follows
Answer: **only II**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The conclusion ends with "is a possibility".
pyqPatterns.approach:
Try to draw one picture where the conclusion is true and all statements still hold.
If you can, it follows.

example.q: Statements: All roads are streets. Some streets are lanes. Conclusion: All lanes being roads is a possibility.
example.solution:
Draw lanes inside roads, and roads inside streets
Some streets are lanes, so that still holds
The picture works, so it **follows**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Neither conclusion follows, but they are opposites of each other (like All and Some not).
pyqPatterns.approach:
Check each conclusion alone first.
Use "Either I or II" only if they are exact opposites and neither follows alone.

example.q: Statements: Some flowers are red. No flower is blue. I. All flowers are red. II. Some flowers are not red.
example.solution:
I does not follow alone, and II does not follow alone
They are exact opposites, so one of them must be true
Answer: **Either I or II follows**

pyqPatterns.approach:
Read it as: some A are B, and some A are not B.
Use only the A that are B when you chain it forward.

example.q: Statements: Only a few cups are plates. All plates are bowls. I. Some cups are not plates. II. No cup is a bowl.
example.solution:
"Only a few" means some cups are not plates, so I follows
The cups that are plates are also bowls, so II is false
Answer: **only I**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The conclusion is a reversed form of a statement.
pyqPatterns.approach:
All A are B gives Some B are A.
Some A are B gives Some B are A; No A is B gives No B is A.

example.q: Statement: All roses are flowers. Conclusion: Some flowers are roses.
example.solution:
Every rose is a flower
So at least some flowers are roses
This always holds, so it **follows**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A conclusion that looks natural but needs a picture you chose.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Move a part of the picture while the statements stay true.
If the conclusion breaks, it does not follow.

example.q: Statement: Some spoons are forks. Conclusion: Some spoons are not forks.
example.solution:
Draw all spoons as forks
The statement still holds
But the conclusion fails, so it **does not follow**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A possibility conclusion, and a "No" statement is close to it.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Find the members that must exist.
If the possibility would put them in a banned group, it fails.

example.q: Statements: Some phones are cameras. No camera is a charger. Conclusion: All phones being chargers is a possibility.
example.solution:
Some phones are cameras, and these phones must exist
No camera is a charger
So not all phones can be chargers: **does not follow**

solvedExamples.q:
**Statements:** All teachers are graduates. Some graduates are postgraduates.

**Conclusions:** I. Some teachers are postgraduates. II. All graduates are teachers.
solvedExamples.solution: Minimal diagram: teachers inside graduates; postgraduates overlapping graduates — possibly away from teachers. That diagram breaks I, so I fails. Postgraduates outside graduates breaks II's premise-side... more directly, graduates extend beyond teachers, so II fails too. **Neither follows.**
solvedExamples.shortcut: Overlap the 'some' circle away from the 'All' circle — that one diagram kills conclusion I; the All arrow never reverses for II.

solvedExamples.q:
**Statements:** All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants.

**Conclusions:** I. All roses are plants. II. Some plants are roses.
solvedExamples.solution: Chain the All's: roses ⊂ flowers ⊂ plants → I follows. Roses are non-empty and sit inside plants, so some plants are roses → II follows. **Both follow.**
solvedExamples.shortcut: All-chains carry forward, and 'All A are B' always gifts you 'Some B are A'.

solvedExamples.q:
**Statement:** Some mangoes are sweet.

**Conclusions:** I. All mangoes are sweet. II. Some mangoes are not sweet.
solvedExamples.solution: I and II are exact negations of each other, so at least one must be true — but the statement alone fixes neither. **Either I or II follows.**
solvedExamples.shortcut: (All …) + (Some … not) on the same terms with no individual proof = either-or.

solvedExamples.q:
**Statements:** All doors are wooden. Some wooden things are brown.

**Conclusions:** I. All doors being brown is a possibility. II. No door is brown.
solvedExamples.solution: I: draw doors inside the brown part of wooden — every statement still holds, so the possibility is consistent → I follows. II: the diagram just built breaks it, and nothing forces doors away from brown either. **Only I follows.**
solvedExamples.shortcut: Possibility = one supporting diagram; II's 'No' isn't forced by anything.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All pens are books. All books are copies.

**Conclusions:** I. All pens are copies. II. Some copies are pens.
practice.solution: pens ⊂ books ⊂ copies gives I. Since pens exist inside copies, II follows too. **Both.**
practice.shortcut: All-chain forward + the free 'Some' reversal.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some dogs are cats. All cats are rats.

**Conclusions:** I. Some dogs are rats. II. All rats are dogs.
practice.solution: The dog-cat overlap sits inside rats, so some dogs are rats — I follows. Rats spread beyond dogs, so II fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Drop the shared element of a Some+All chain into the third term.

practice.q:
**Statements:** No glass is metal. Some metals are solids.

**Conclusions:** I. Some solids are not glass. II. All glasses are solids.
practice.solution: The solid that is metal cannot be glass (glass and metal never meet) → some solids are not glass: I follows. Glass has no forced link with solids → II fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: A 'Some metal are solid' element inherits metal's full exile from glass.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some flowers are red. No flower is blue.

**Conclusions:** I. All flowers are red. II. Some flowers are not red.
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: The red part of flowers isn't fixed as all or some-not, so neither conclusion is provable — but they are exact negations, so one of them must hold. **Either-or.**
practice.shortcut: (All, Some-not) pair on the same terms = complementary.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All cars are buses. Some trucks are buses.

**Conclusions:** I. Some cars are trucks. II. No car is a truck.
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: Cars sit inside buses, trucks somewhere in buses too — but the statements never fix whether cars meet trucks. I and II are exact negations of each other, so they cannot both fail. **Either-or.**
practice.shortcut: Same two terms, (Some …) vs (No …), neither provable → complementary pair.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some apples are mangoes. No mango is a banana.

**Conclusions:** I. All apples being bananas is a possibility. II. Some apples are not bananas.
practice.solution: I: an apple-mango element can never be a banana, so filling all apples into bananas is impossible → I fails. II: that same apple-mango element is an apple outside bananas → II follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: The shared 'Some' element must obey BOTH statements — trace it through.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All roads are streets. Some streets are lanes.

**Conclusions:** I. All lanes being roads is a possibility. II. Some lanes are not streets.
practice.solution: I: draw lanes inside roads (roads inside streets) — consistent with both statements → possibility holds. II: the lane-street overlap may cover all lanes, so II isn't forced. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Possibility needs one friendly diagram; here nothing blocks it.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All keys are locks. Some locks are doors. No door is a window.

**Conclusions:** I. Some keys are doors. II. Some locks are not windows.
practice.solution: I: the lock-door overlap can sit outside the keys region → not forced. II: the lock that is a door cannot be a window → that lock is 'a lock not a window' → follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: Carry the Some-element through both of its statements before judging.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Only a few cups are plates. All plates are bowls.

**Conclusions:** I. Some cups are not plates. II. No cup is a bowl.
practice.solution: 'Only a few' guarantees a part of cups outside plates → I follows. The non-plate cups may still be bowls, and the plate-cups ARE bowls — so II fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Only a few = Some + Some-not, nothing about the other circle.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All chairs are tables. Some tables are desks.

**Conclusions:** I. Some chairs are desks. II. All desks being chairs is a possibility.
practice.solution: I: the table-desk overlap can avoid chairs entirely → fails. II: desks can be drawn inside chairs (chairs inside tables) — fully consistent → possibility follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: Possibility: try to draw it; only a crossing 'No' can stop you.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some pages are files. No file is a folder.

**Conclusions:** I. Some pages are folders. II. All pages being files is a possibility.
practice.solution: I: pages outside files can sit inside folders, and the file-pages cannot — so 'some pages are folders' is possible but not necessary → not a definite follow. II: all pages inside files keeps every statement true → possibility follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: A possibility can hold for a part no statement pins down.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All rings are circles. Some circles are squares. No square is a triangle.

**Conclusions:** I. Some circles are triangles. II. No circle is a triangle.
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: Neither I nor II is forced (circles may or may not touch triangles). They are negation pairs about circles-triangles, so they can't both fail. **Either-or.**
practice.shortcut: Even with three statements, the pair test only needs the two conclusion terms.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some numbers are letters. All letters are symbols. No symbol is a digit.

**Conclusions:** I. Some numbers are not digits. II. All letters are digits.
practice.solution: A number-letter element is a letter → symbol → never a digit → I follows. II collides head-on with 'No symbol is a digit' → fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: One shared element propagated through three statements settles I.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All squares are rectangles. No rectangle is a circle.

**Conclusions:** I. No square is a circle. II. Some circles are not squares.
practice.solution: Squares live inside rectangles, and rectangles never meet circles → no square meets a circle: I follows. Circles are non-empty and entirely outside rectangles, hence entirely outside squares → at least one circle is not a square: II follows too. **Both.**
practice.shortcut: A full exile (No) plus non-emptiness gives you a free 'Some … not' conclusion.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All villages are towns. Only a few towns are cities.

**Conclusions:** I. Some villages are cities. II. All villages being cities is a possibility.
practice.solution: I: the town-city overlap can sit entirely outside the villages → not forced. II: villages can be drawn inside the city-part of towns — consistent with 'only a few' (some towns stay outside cities) → possibility follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: 'Only a few' says the city-part is small, never where your subject sits.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some chairs are tables. All tables are desks.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some chairs are desks.
II. Some desks are chairs.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: The chair-that-is-a-table is a desk, so I follows; II is the free conversion of I, so it follows too. **Both follow.**
practice.shortcut: Some+All: the shared member travels; then convert freely.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some kings are queens. All queens are wise.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some kings are wise.
II. All wise people are kings.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: The king-queen member is wise → I follows. 'All wise are kings' reverses an All → breakable → fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Chain the Some member through the All; never reverse an All.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All stones are rocks. All rocks are minerals.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some minerals are stones.
II. All minerals are rocks.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: Stones ⊂ rocks ⊂ minerals, and stones exist, so some minerals are stones → I follows. Minerals extend beyond rocks → II fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: All-chain forward + the free conversion; the chain never runs backwards.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All telephones are devices. All devices are gadgets. Some gadgets are toys.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some telephones are toys.
II. All telephones are gadgets.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: The gadget-toy overlap can sit entirely outside telephones → I fails. The chain gives telephones ⊂ gadgets → II follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: The All-chain is certain; a Some on a far pair is never forced.

practice.q:
**Statements:** No lizard is a bird. Some birds are black.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some black things are not lizards.
II. All black things are birds.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: The black bird cannot be a lizard → I follows. Black things may include non-birds → II fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: The shared Some member inherits the No statement's exile.

practice.q:
**Statements:** No pen is a pencil. All pencils are stationery.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some stationery is not a pen.
II. No stationery is a pen.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: Every pencil is stationery and no pencil is a pen → those stationery items are not pens → I follows. Stationery (other items) may well include pens → II fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: No + All chain: the pencil block inside stationery is permanently pen-free.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All actors are artists.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some artists are actors.
II. All artists are actors.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: All→Some conversion always follows (classes are never empty). The reverse All is not implied. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Conversion of All = free Some; the reverse All is the trap.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some singers are dancers.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some dancers are singers.
II. Some singers are not dancers.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I is the plain conversion → follows. II is possible but never forced (all singers could be dancers) → fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Some converts both ways; Some never gives Some-not.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All windows are doors. Some doors are gates.

**Conclusions:**
I. All gates being windows is a possibility.
II. Some windows are gates.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I: draw gates inside windows, windows inside doors, with extra doors outside — consistent → follows. II: the door-gate overlap can avoid windows → not forced. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Possibility needs one clean diagram; a Some overlap is never forced onto a third class.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some spoons are forks.

**Conclusions:**
I. All forks being spoons is a possibility.
II. No fork is a spoon.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I: draw all forks inside spoons — the Some overlap survives → follows. II is a definite No, nothing forces it → fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: With a lone Some statement, almost every possibility passes.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All cups are vessels. No vessel is a rod.

**Conclusions:**
I. All cups being rods is a possibility.
II. Some vessels are not cups.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I: cups sit inside vessels, and vessels never meet rods — so cups can never be rods → impossible. II: vessels could all be cups (nothing says otherwise) → not forced. **Neither follows.**
practice.shortcut: A No statement across the possibility's terms kills it; outside classes stay free.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some phones are cameras. No camera is a charger.

**Conclusions:**
I. All phones being chargers is a possibility.
II. Some phones are not chargers.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: The phone-camera member is a camera, so it can never be a charger → I is impossible. That same member is a phone outside chargers → II follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: Trace the Some member through the No statement — it settles both conclusions.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Only a few chairs are sofas. All sofas are furniture.

**Conclusions:**
I. All chairs being furniture is a possibility.
II. Some chairs are not sofas.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I: draw every chair inside furniture (sofa-chairs are furniture, the rest join freely) — consistent → follows. II: guaranteed by only-a-few → follows. **Both.**
practice.shortcut: Only-a-few kills only 'All A are B'; other possibilities stay open.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Only a few pens are markers.

**Conclusions:**
I. All pens being markers is a possibility.
II. Some pens are not markers.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: Only-a-few guarantees pens outside markers, so all-pens-inside-markers is impossible → I fails. II is the guaranteed half → follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: 'All … is a possibility' dies the moment an only-a-few touches the same pair.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All shirts are clothes. Some clothes are expensive.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some shirts are expensive.
II. All expensive things being shirts is a possibility.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I: the clothes-expensive overlap can dodge shirts → fails. II: draw all expensive things inside shirts (shirts inside clothes) — every statement holds → follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: Definite and possibility use different standards — judge each on its own.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some books are novels. All novels are stories.

**Conclusions:**
I. All books being stories is a possibility.
II. Some stories are books.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I: draw all books inside stories (the book-novel part already is; the rest joins) → follows. II: the book-novel member is a story → follows definitely. **Both.**
practice.shortcut: A possibility passes when no No statement is near; the Some member still gifts a definite.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some candles are lamps.

**Conclusions:**
I. All candles are lamps.
II. Some candles are not lamps.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: Neither half is forced by a lone Some statement, and they are exact negations about candles–lamps. **Either I or II follows.**
practice.shortcut: (All, Some-not) on the same terms with no individual proof = either-or.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All shirts are cotton.

**Conclusions:**
I. All shirts are white.
II. Some shirts are not white.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: Nothing links shirts with white, so neither follows alone; the pair is a true negation pair. **Either I or II follows.**
practice.shortcut: The statements may ignore the pair completely — the pair rule still works.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some rings are gold.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some rings are silver.
II. No ring is silver.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: Gold is a decoy — silver is untouched, so neither conclusion is provable. Some/No on the same pair = complementary. **Either I or II follows.**
practice.shortcut: Ignore the unused statement; judge only the conclusion pair.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All keys are metal. Some metal is heavy.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some keys are iron.
II. No key is iron.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: Iron is never mentioned in the statements, so keys–iron stays open; the Some/No pair covers it. **Either I or II follows.**
practice.shortcut: Three statements cannot close a pair the statements never touch.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some cups are plates.

**Conclusions:**
I. All cups are bowls.
II. Some cups are not plates.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: The two conclusions look like an (All, Some-not) pair, but they use different second terms (bowls vs plates). A world with all cups inside plates and outside bowls fails both. **Neither follows.**
practice.shortcut: Same-shape pair with mismatched terms is the classic fake — check the terms word by word.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some pencils are erasers.

**Conclusions:**
I. No pencil is an eraser.
II. Some pencils are not erasers.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: I is contradicted by the statement. II is not forced. And both can fail together (all pencils are erasers) — No + Some-not is NOT a negation pair. **Neither follows.**
practice.shortcut: (No, Some-not) is the fake pair students fall for; only (All, Some-not) and (Some, No) work.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All beds are sofas.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some sofas are beds.
II. No sofa is a bed.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: I follows at once by conversion (All→Some). Once one conclusion follows alone, never mark either-or, however tempting the pair looks. **Only I follows.**
practice.shortcut: Step order: test each conclusion alone BEFORE using the either-or shortcut.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Some windows are glass. All glass is transparent.

**Conclusions:**
I. All windows are glass.
II. Some windows are not glass.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: The transparent chain does not pin windows fully inside or outside glass. Neither follows alone; the (All, Some-not) pair does. **Either I or II follows.**
practice.shortcut: Extra true statements cannot create a third option for a negation pair.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All squares are rectangles. Some rectangles are big. No big thing is small.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some squares are small.
II. No square is small.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
practice.solution: Squares may or may not be big, so their link with small stays open — neither follows alone. The Some/No pair is complementary. **Either I or II follows.**
practice.shortcut: Chain what you can; if the pair's terms stay undecided, mark either-or.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Only a few mangoes are sweet.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some mangoes are sweet.
II. All mangoes are sweet.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: Only-a-few = Some + Some-not, so I follows. II is contradicted by the guaranteed non-sweet part. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Split 'only a few' the moment you read it.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Only a few books are novels.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some books are not novels.
II. Some novels are books.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I is the guaranteed outside part → follows. II converts the Some half → follows. **Both.**
practice.shortcut: Only-a-few gifts two conclusions: the split pair and its conversion.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Only a few cups are plates. All plates are dishes.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some cups are dishes.
II. Some cups are not dishes.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: The cup-that-is-a-plate is a dish → I follows. The non-plate cups may still be dishes → II fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Only the B-side member chains through the All; the outside member stays free.

practice.q:
**Statements:** All chairs are furniture. Only a few furniture items are costly.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some chairs are costly.
II. All costly things being furniture is a possibility.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I: the furniture-costly overlap can sit outside chairs → fails. II: draw all costly things inside chairs (chairs inside furniture, some furniture outside) → consistent → follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: Only-a-few pins the split on ITS subject side only — everything else can be drawn freely.

practice.q:
**Statements:** A few students are athletes. All athletes are fit.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some students are fit.
II. All students are athletes.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: 'A few' = plain Some: the student-athlete is fit → I follows. II is the reverse-All trap. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: No guaranteed outside part with 'a few' — do not import only-a-few rules.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Many Indian cities have metro rails.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some Indian cities have metro rails.
II. All Indian cities have metro rails.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: 'Many' = Some, so I follows. II overreaches — many is not all. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Many / a few / some are one and the same in syllogisms.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Only a few roads are wide. All wide roads are smooth.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some roads are smooth.
II. All roads being smooth is a possibility.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I: the road-that-is-wide is smooth → follows. II: draw all roads inside smooth (wide roads already are; non-wide roads join) → consistent → follows. **Both.**
practice.shortcut: A possibility passes as long as no guaranteed member collides with it.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Only a few workers are skilled.

**Conclusions:**
I. No worker is skilled.
II. Some workers are skilled.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: Only-a-few asserts the overlap, so No is contradicted → I fails; II is its Some half → follows. **Only II.**
practice.shortcut: 'Only a few' never means 'none' — the overlap is asserted, not denied.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Only a few flowers are fragrant.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some fragrant things are flowers.
II. All fragrant things are flowers.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: I converts the Some half → follows. The fragrant class may spread far beyond flowers → II fails. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: The B-side is never fixed by only-a-few — no All, no Some-not on that side.

practice.q:
**Statements:** Only a few keys are brass. All brass items are metal. No metal is plastic.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some keys are not plastic.
II. All keys being plastic is a possibility.

Which of the conclusions follow(s)?
practice.solution: The key-that-is-brass is metal, hence never plastic — that key is 'a key not a plastic' → I follows. The same key blocks all keys inside plastic → II is impossible. **Only I.**
practice.shortcut: Trace the only-a-few member through the All into the No — one journey settles both.
